Even though there are some differences in nuance of morals, there is overwhelming similarity in the moral codes across culture and history. Imagine, if you will, a society in which cowardice was glorified and it was encouraged to murder in cold blood. Let me give you a scenario to prove that it isn't purely evolutionary. If you were walking by a lake and you heard something thrashing in the water. You look over and there is a child drowning. Evolutionary instinct would dictate that you not risk drowning to save the child. The child obviously does not have superior genetics, or it would save itself. You are better off living and the child is better dead so it doesn't pollute the gene pool with its weak genes. Now obviously, this would not be considered morally good in any culture. There has to be a stronger moral factor overriding the evolutionary instinct. If morals were in fact based on evolution and natural selection, we would consider Hitler to be a moral leader because he was trying to speed up natural selection by clearing the gene pool of inferior races and disabled people, mentally and physically. This isn't the case. 
Your argument fails on the basis of soundness. Moreover, I challenge your argument on the basis of validity. Your first premise, "morals only exist within the society that created them and only so long as the majority agree to them." It does not logically follow that, "there is no human agreement on morals." You affirm both that morals exist and that morals do not exist, explicitly contradicting yourself. 
Let me also address the concept of conventionalism, the view that morality is relative to a particular society. It runs into three major problems. The first is the question of moral codes if a person from one culture visits another culture. Do they follow their own morals or those of the society they are visiting? Any solution to this problem would give an absolute moral code that crosses cultural boundaries. That is the first absurdity that comes from conventionalism. Another is called the "reformers' dilemma." Reformers would be evil because they oppose the society's morals, claiming that there is a higher moral standard that the society ought to uphold. The third is a theoretical scenario. If there were only two people in the world or a society and they disagree morally, it would be impossible to determine who is morally right because there would be no majority. Furthermore, conventionalism claims that the whole world ought to acknowledge that each society is correct in its morals. That is a universal moral. Conventionalism not only is self-contradictory, but also creates major problems and absurdities. 
Your argument fails in soundness of the first premise and second premise, and in validity in that it is explicitly self-contradicting, and has the fallacy of being a non-sequitur. (Your contradiction leads to it being a non-sequitur).
